\chapter{Chapter03 — Vector Fourier}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from FABL.Chapter03.SubspacesAndDecisionTrees.VectorFourier
\section{Overview}

Declarations of the Lean module \texttt{FABL.Chapter03.SubspacesAndDecisionTrees.VectorFourier}.

\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Binary support]
\lean{FABL.f₂Support}
\leanok
For a vector $\gamma$ in the $n$-dimensional binary cube, define its support to be the
set of coordinates where its value is nonzero.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Membership in the binary support]
\lean{FABL.mem_f₂Support}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.f₂Support}
\difficulty{1}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $\gamma$ be a function from the $n$-dimensional binary
cube to the two-element field, and let $i\text{Fin}(n)$. Then $i$ belongs to the support
of $\gamma$ exactly when $\gamma(i)$ is nonzero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Binary vector of a finite set]
\lean{FABL.f₂CubeOfFinset}
\leanok
For a set $S$ of coordinates among the $n$ coordinates, define its binary vector to have
value $1$ on coordinates in $S$ and value $0$ on coordinates outside $S$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Coordinates of a set indicator]
\lean{FABL.f₂CubeOfFinset_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.f₂CubeOfFinset}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$, every finite set $S\subseteq\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, and every
$i\in\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, the $i$th coordinate of its binary indicator vector is $1$ if
$i\in S$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Binary cube and finite subsets]
\lean{FABL.f₂CubeEquivFinset}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.f₂CubeOfFinset, FABL.f₂Support}
For each natural number $n$, the support map gives an equivalence between the
$n$-dimensional cube over the field with two elements and the finite subsets of
$	ext{Fin}(n)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Support of a binary vector]
\lean{FABL.f₂CubeEquivFinset_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.f₂CubeEquivFinset, FABL.f₂Support}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$ and every vector $\gamma\in(\mathbb{F}_2)^n$, the finite
set corresponding to $\gamma$ under the binary-cube-to-finite-set equivalence is exactly
$\{i\in\mathrm{Fin}(n):\gamma_i\ne0\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Binary vector associated to a finite set]
\lean{FABL.f₂CubeEquivFinset_symm_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.f₂CubeEquivFinset, FABL.f₂CubeOfFinset}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$ and every finite set $S\subseteq\mathrm{Fin}(n)$, the
inverse of the binary-cube-to-finite-set equivalence sends $S$ to the vector whose $i$th
coordinate is $1$ when $i\in S$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Dot product as a sum over the support]
\lean{FABL.f₂DotProduct_eq_coordinateSum_f₂Support}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.coordinateSum, FABL.f₂DotProduct, FABL.f₂Support}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $\gamma,x\in\bbr_2^n$. The dot product of
$\gamma$ and $x$ equals the sum of the coordinates of $x$ at precisely those indices
where $\gamma$ is nonzero, with the sum taken in $\bbr_2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Vector Walsh character]
\lean{FABL.vectorWalshCharacter}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p023-b001,

\label{FABL.vectorWalshCharacter}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.f₂Support, FABL.χ}
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $\gamma\in(\mathbb{F}_2)^n$. The vector Walsh character
indexed by $\gamma$ is the character associated with the support of $\gamma$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{3}
For $\gamma,x\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$, the vector Walsh character indexed by $\gamma$ and
evaluated at $x$ equals the binary sign character applied to the dot product
$\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_i x_i$ in $\mathbb{F}_2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Walsh character of a singleton frequency]
\lean{FABL.vectorWalshCharacter_f₂CubeOfFinset_singleton}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binarySign, FABL.coordinateSum, FABL.f₂CubeEquivFinset, FABL.f₂CubeOfFinset, FABL.f₂Support, FABL.vectorWalshCharacter, FABL.χ}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $i\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$, and let $x\in\mathbb
F_2^n$. The Walsh character indexed by the vector that is $1$ at coordinate $i$ and $0$
elsewhere, evaluated at $x$, equals the binary sign of $x_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[When the binary sign is one]
\lean{FABL.binarySign_eq_one_iff}
\label{FABL.binarySign_eq_one_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binarySign, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{4}
For every $b\in\mathbb{F}_2$, the binary sign of $b$ equals $1$ if and only if $b=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sign encoding of zero]
\lean{FABL.signEncode_zero}
\label{FABL.signEncode_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.signEncode, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{1}
The sign encoding of $0\in\mathbb{F}_2$ is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sign encoding of one]
\lean{FABL.signEncode_one}
\label{FABL.signEncode_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.signEncode, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{1}
The sign encoding of $1\in\mathbb{F}_2$ is $-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Binary sign of one]
\lean{FABL.binarySign_one}
\label{FABL.binarySign_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binarySign, FABL.signEncode_one, FABL.signValue_neg_one, FABL.signValue_signEncode_eq_binarySign, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{3}
The binary sign of $1\in\mathbb{F}_2$ is $-1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Values of binary Walsh characters]
\lean{FABL.vectorWalshCharacter_eq_neg_one_or_one}
\label{FABL.vectorWalshCharacter_eq_neg_one_or_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.f₂DotProduct, FABL.vectorWalshCharacter, FABL.vectorWalshCharacter_apply}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $\gamma,x\in\mathbb F_2^n$. The Walsh character
indexed by $\gamma$, evaluated at $x$, is either $-1$ or $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Magnitude of a binary Walsh character]
\lean{FABL.abs_vectorWalshCharacter}
\label{FABL.abs_vectorWalshCharacter}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.vectorWalshCharacter, FABL.vectorWalshCharacter_eq_neg_one_or_one}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$ and every $\gamma,x\in\mathbb F_2^n$, the absolute value of
the Walsh character indexed by $\gamma$, evaluated at $x$, is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Binary values and signs]
\lean{FABL.binarySignEquiv}
\label{FABL.binarySignEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.signEncode, FABL.𝔽₂}
The map sending the two elements of the field with two elements to the two units of the
integers defines an equivalence between these sets.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Binary cube and sign cube]
\lean{FABL.binaryCubeSignEquiv}
\label{FABL.binaryCubeSignEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binarySignEquiv}
For each natural number $n$, applying the binary-to-sign equivalence independently in
every coordinate gives an equivalence between the $n$-dimensional binary cube and the
$n$-dimensional sign cube.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Coordinate formula for the sign encoding]
\lean{FABL.binaryCubeSignEquiv_apply}
\label{FABL.binaryCubeSignEquiv_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binaryCubeSignEquiv, FABL.signEncode}
\difficulty{1}
For every binary vector $x$ of length $n$ and every coordinate $i$, the $i$th coordinate
of its sign encoding is $(-1)^{x_i}$, viewed as a sign in $\{ -1,1\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Monomial binary cube sign equiv]
\lean{FABL.monomial_binaryCubeSignEquiv}

}

\difficulty{4}

\begin{definition}[Function on the sign cube]
\lean{FABL.binaryFunctionOnSignCube}
\statementsource{ghsz-combinatorial-list-decoding}{pdf-6bd33ae73ade-p005-b002}
\label{FABL.binaryFunctionOnSignCube}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binaryCubeSignEquiv}
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $f:(\mathbb{F}_2)^n\to\mathbb{R}$. The corresponding
function on the sign cube $\{-1,1\}^n$ sends each sign vector to the value of $f$ at its
inverse image under the binary-to-sign cube bijection.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$, every real-valued function $f$ on the binary cube
$(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n$, and every set of coordinates $S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$,
the Fourier coefficient of the function on the sign cube obtained from $f$ by binary
sign encoding at $S$ equals the binary Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $S$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Walsh character at the zero index]
\lean{FABL.vectorWalshCharacter_zero}
\label{FABL.vectorWalshCharacter_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.f₂DotProduct, FABL.vectorWalshCharacter, FABL.vectorWalshCharacter_apply}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$, the Walsh character indexed by the zero vector in $\mathbb
F_2^n$ is the constant character with value $1$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $\beta,\gamma\in\mathbb F_2^n$. The pointwise
product of the Walsh characters indexed by $\beta$ and $\gamma$ is the Walsh character
indexed by $\beta+\gamma$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Vector Fourier coefficient]
\lean{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p025-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p072-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p157-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p240-b008
}
\statementsource{ghsz-combinatorial-list-decoding}{pdf-6bd33ae73ade-p005-b002}
\label{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binaryFourierCoeff, FABL.f₂Support}
For a function $f:]\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{R}$ and a vector
$\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$, its vector Fourier coefficient is the binary Fourier
coefficient of $f$ indexed by the support of $\gamma$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficients under the sign-cube identification]
\lean{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_eq_fourierCoeff_binaryFunctionOnSignCube}
\label{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_eq_fourierCoeff_binaryFunctionOnSignCube}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binaryFunctionOnSignCube, FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierCoeff_binaryFunctionOnSignCube, FABL.f₂Support, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff}
\difficulty{1}
Let $f\colon\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb R$ and $\gamma\in\mathbb F_2^n$. The vector Fourier
coefficient of $f$ at $\gamma$ equals the Fourier coefficient, on the sign cube
$\{-1,1\}^n$, of the function obtained by transporting $f$ through the coordinatewise
identification of binary vectors with signs, at the monomial indexed by the support of
$\gamma$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{1}
Let $f\colon\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb R$ and $\gamma\in\mathbb F_2^n$. Its vector Fourier
coefficient at $\gamma$ equals the uniform expectation over $x\in\mathbb F_2^n$ of
$f(x)$ times the Walsh character associated with the support of $\gamma$, evaluated at
$x$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb R$, and let $x\in\mathbb
F_2^n$. Then $f(x)=\sum_{\gamma\in\mathbb F_2^n}\widehat f(\gamma)\chi_\gamma(x)$, where
$\widehat f(\gamma)$ is the uniform average of $f(z)\chi_\gamma(z)$ over $z\in\mathbb
F_2^n$ and $\chi_\gamma$ is the Walsh character indexed by $\gamma$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f,g:\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb R$. The uniform average
of $f(x)g(x)$ over $x\in\mathbb F_2^n$ equals $\sum_{\gamma\in\mathbb F_2^n}\widehat
f(\gamma)\widehat g(\gamma)$, where each Fourier coefficient is the uniform average of
the function times the Walsh character indexed by $\gamma$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Spectral p quantity]
\lean{FABL.spectralPNorm}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p013-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p072-b001
}
\label{FABL.spectralPNorm}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff}
For $p\in\mathbb{R}$ and $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{R}$, define the spectral $p$
quantity as $\left(\sum_{\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_2^n}|\widehat f(\gamma)|^p\right)^{1/p}$,
where $\widehat f(\gamma)$ denotes the vector Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $\gamma$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{4}
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let $f:(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n\to\mathbb{R}$. The uniform
$2$-norm of $f$ equals the $2$-norm of its Fourier spectrum, the vector of Fourier
coefficients indexed by $(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})^n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Spectral infinity norm]
\lean{FABL.spectralInfinityNorm}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p086-b009}
\label{FABL.spectralInfinityNorm}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff}
For $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{R}$, define its spectral infinity norm to be
$\max_{\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_2^n}|\widehat f(\gamma)|$, where $\widehat f(\gamma)$ is its
vector Fourier coefficient at $\gamma$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Spectral sparsity]
\lean{FABL.spectralSparsity}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p072-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p086-b015,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p091-b003
}
\label{FABL.spectralSparsity}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff}
For $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{R}$, its spectral sparsity is the number of vectors
$\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$ for which the vector Fourier coefficient $\widehat f(\gamma)$
is nonzero.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Vector Fourier support]
\lean{FABL.vectorFourierSupport}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p018-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p091-b003
}
\label{FABL.vectorFourierSupport}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff}
For $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{R}$, its vector Fourier support is the set of vectors
$\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$ for which the vector Fourier coefficient $\widehat f(\gamma)$
is nonzero.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Characterization of Fourier support]
\lean{FABL.mem_vectorFourierSupport}
\label{FABL.mem_vectorFourierSupport}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff, FABL.vectorFourierSupport}
\difficulty{1}
For a real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional vector space over the field with
two elements and a vector $\gamma$ in that space, $\gamma$ belongs to the vector Fourier
support of $f$ if and only if its vector Fourier coefficient is nonzero.
\end{theorem}

\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p072-b002}
\label{FABL.spectralSparsity_eq_card_vectorFourierSupport}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.spectralSparsity, FABL.vectorFourierSupport}

\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Vector Fourier granularity]
\lean{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p072-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p089-b003
}
\label{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsFourierGranular, FABL.binaryFunctionOnSignCube}
A function $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is vector Fourier granular with parameter
$\varepsilon\in\mathbb{R}$ if the function on the sign cube induced by $f$ is Fourier
granular with parameter $\varepsilon$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Is vector fourier granular iff]
\lean{FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_iff}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p072-b003}

\leanok

\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Vector Fourier degree]
\lean{FABL.vectorFourierDegree}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p028-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p036-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p088-b006
}
\label{FABL.vectorFourierDegree}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binaryFunctionOnSignCube, FABL.fourierDegree}
For $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{R}$, its vector Fourier degree is the Fourier degree of
the function on the sign cube induced by $f$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Vector fourier degree le iff]
\lean{FABL.vectorFourierDegree_le_iff}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p036-b002}
\label{FABL.vectorFourierDegree_le_iff}
\leanok

\begin{definition}[Supremum norm on the binary cube]
\lean{FABL.binaryFunctionInfinityNorm}
\label{FABL.binaryFunctionInfinityNorm}
\leanok
For a real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional binary cube, its infinity norm is
the maximum of $|f(x)|$ over all cube points $x$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Pointwise bound by the binary-function supremum norm]
\lean{FABL.abs_le_binaryFunctionInfinityNorm}
\label{FABL.abs_le_binaryFunctionInfinityNorm}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binaryFunctionInfinityNorm}
\difficulty{1}
For a real-valued function $f$ on the binary cube and any point $x$ in that cube,
$|f(x)|$ is at most the supremum of $|f|$ over the cube.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Additivity of vector Fourier coefficients]
\lean{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_add}
\label{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_add}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_eq_expect}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$, every pair of real-valued functions $f,g$ on
$\mathbb{F}_2^n$, and every $\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$, the vector Fourier coefficient of
$f+g$ at $\gamma$ is the sum of the vector Fourier coefficients of $f$ and $g$ at
$\gamma$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Scaling a Fourier coefficient]
\lean{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_const_mul}
\label{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_const_mul}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.vectorFourierCoeff, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_eq_expect, FABL.vectorWalshCharacter}
\difficulty{3}
Let $c\in\mathbb R$, let $f\colon\mathbb F_2^n\to\mathbb R$, and let $\gamma\in\mathbb
F_2^n$. The vector Fourier coefficient of the function $x\mapsto c f(x)$ at $\gamma$
equals $c$ times the vector Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $\gamma$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Granularity of the zero function]
\lean{FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_zero}
\label{FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular, FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_iff, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_eq_expect}
\difficulty{3}
For every real number $\varepsilon$, the zero function on the $n$-dimensional cube over
$\bbf_2$ is vector Fourier granular with granularity $\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Addition preserves Fourier granularity]
\lean{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular.add}
\label{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular.add}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular, FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_iff, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_add}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f,g:\mathbb{F}_2^n	o\mathbb{R}$ have the property that every Fourier coefficient of each function,
after identifying the binary cube with the sign cube, is an integer multiple of the same
real number $\varepsilon$. Then every such Fourier coefficient of $f+g$ is also an
integer multiple of $\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Integer scaling preserves Fourier granularity]
\lean{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular.intCast_mul}
\label{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular.intCast_mul}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular, FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_iff, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_const_mul}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n	o\mathbb{R}$ have the property that every Fourier coefficient of its corresponding
function on the sign cube is an integer multiple of $\varepsilon$. For every integer
$a$, the function $x	o a f(x)$ has the same property.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Refining Fourier granularity]
\lean{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular.refine}
\label{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular.refine}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular, FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_iff}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n	o\mathbb{R}$ have the property that every Fourier coefficient of its corresponding
function on the sign cube is an integer multiple of $\delta$. Suppose an integer $q$
satisfies $\delta=q\varepsilon$. Then every such Fourier coefficient of $f$ is an
integer multiple of $\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Identity for reciprocal powers of two]
\lean{FABL.inverse_two_pow_eq_natCast_mul_inverse_two_pow}
\label{FABL.inverse_two_pow_eq_natCast_mul_inverse_two_pow}
\leanok
\difficulty{4}
Let $\ell$ and $k$ be nonnegative integers with $\ell\le k$. Then
$2^{-\ell}=2^{k-\ell}2^{-k}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Support of a sum of functions]
\lean{FABL.vectorFourierSupport_add_subset}
\label{FABL.vectorFourierSupport_add_subset}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.mem_vectorFourierSupport, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_add, FABL.vectorFourierSupport}
\difficulty{4}
For real-valued functions $f,g$ on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, the vector Fourier support of $f+g$
is contained in the union of the vector Fourier supports of $f$ and $g$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Support under scalar multiplication]
\lean{FABL.vectorFourierSupport_const_mul_subset}
\label{FABL.vectorFourierSupport_const_mul_subset}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.mem_vectorFourierSupport, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_const_mul, FABL.vectorFourierSupport}
\difficulty{3}
For any real number $c$ and real-valued function $f$ on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$, the vector
Fourier support of the function $x\mapsto c f(x)$ is contained in the vector Fourier
support of $f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Subadditivity of spectral sparsity]
\lean{FABL.spectralSparsity_add_le}
\label{FABL.spectralSparsity_add_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.spectralSparsity, FABL.spectralSparsity_eq_card_vectorFourierSupport, FABL.vectorFourierSupport_add_subset}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, and let $f$ and $g$ be real-valued functions on the
$n$-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb F_2$. The spectral sparsity of their sum is
at most the sum of their spectral sparsities.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Spectral sparsity under scalar multiplication]
\lean{FABL.spectralSparsity_const_mul_le}
\label{FABL.spectralSparsity_const_mul_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.spectralSparsity, FABL.spectralSparsity_eq_card_vectorFourierSupport, FABL.vectorFourierSupport_const_mul_subset}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $c$ be real, and let $f$ be a real-valued function
on the $n$-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb F_2$. The spectral sparsity of the
function $x\mapsto c f(x)$ is at most the spectral sparsity of $f$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{3}
For every real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$,
its spectral one-norm equals the sum, over all vectors in that space, of the absolute
values of its Fourier coefficients.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Triangle inequality for the spectral one-norm]
\lean{FABL.spectralPNorm_one_add_le}
\label{FABL.spectralPNorm_one_add_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.spectralPNorm, FABL.spectralPNorm_one_eq_sum_abs, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_add}
\difficulty{4}
For every pair of real-valued functions $f,g$ on the $n$-dimensional vector space over
$\mathbb{F}_2$, the spectral one-norm of $f+g$ is at most the sum of their spectral
one-norms.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Homogeneity of the spectral one-norm]
\lean{FABL.spectralPNorm_one_const_mul}
\label{FABL.spectralPNorm_one_const_mul}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.spectralPNorm, FABL.spectralPNorm_one_eq_sum_abs, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_const_mul}
\difficulty{3}
For every real number $c$ and every real-valued function $f$ on the $n$-dimensional
vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$, the spectral one-norm of the function $x\mapsto c f(x)$
equals $|c|$ times the spectral one-norm of $f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Nonnegativity of the infinity norm]
\lean{FABL.binaryFunctionInfinityNorm_nonneg}
\label{FABL.binaryFunctionInfinityNorm_nonneg}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.abs_le_binaryFunctionInfinityNorm, FABL.binaryFunctionInfinityNorm}
\difficulty{1}
For every dimension $n$ and every real-valued function $f$ on the binary cube of
dimension $n$, its infinity norm is nonnegative.
\end{theorem}
